system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2186-06-16 07:15:00 to 2186-06-17 13:40:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of gastroparesis, multiple abdominal surgeries, and chronic leukocytosis was admitted for abdominal pain and nausea consistent with a gastroparesis flare. Imaging showed no obstruction or acute abdominal process, and infectious workup was negative. She was managed with NPO status, GJ tube feeds, and symptom control using morphine and lorazepam. Her leukocytosis persisted but was deemed chronic and non-infectious. Hypertension was addressed with initiation of lisinopril, titrated to 40 mg daily. TSH was mildly elevated at 6.0, likely due to malabsorption or illness, with plans to recheck as an outpatient. She improved clinically, advanced to a regular diet, and was discharged home with follow-up arranged in GI and primary care.

storyline_prompt_block:
Discharge note 1 (2186-06-17 00:00:00): Name:  ___              Unit No:   ___
 
Admission Date:  ___              Discharge Date:   ___
 
Date of Birth:  ___             Sex:   F
 
Service: SURGERY
 
Allergies: 
No Known Allergies / Adverse Drug Reactions
 
Attending: ___
 
Chief Complaint:
recurrent left breast cancer
 
Major Surgical or Invasive Procedure:
1. left total mastectomy

 
History of Present Illness:
Ms. ___ is a very pleasant
___ female who was previously seen in Breast Surgery
Clinic on ___, to discuss the new diagnosis of left
breast recurrent carcinoma.

Her past medical and past surgical history is significant for
left breast cancer diagnosed in ___ and treated at ___. 
Per outside records, she had an infiltrating carcinoma of the
left breast with a lumpectomy followed by a reexcision and an
axillary lymph node dissection of 17 nodes showing all of them
negative for carcinoma.  Thereafter, she underwent adjuvant
radiation therapy at ___.  No endocrine or
chemotherapy was given thereafter.

More recently, calcifications in the right breast were being
watched on mammogram in the retroareolar region.  In ___,
her mammogram showed a new asymmetry in the superior posterior
aspect of the left breast for which additional imaging was
recommended.  She had an ill-defined hypoechoic shadowing
measuring 1 cm in size at the 11 to 12 o'clock position in the
left breast.  She underwent image-guided core biopsy of the left
breast lesion on ___, resulting as invasive lobular
carcinoma, grade 2 with receptors pending.  She was thus
diagnosed with recurrent left breast carcinoma and presented to
our Breast Surgery Clinic at that time to discuss the clinical
and surgical treatment plan.

We discussed options for management.  At the time of her visit
with us, we did not receive her outside imaging and thus cannot
have it reviewed at our institution.  Subsequently, it has
arrived.  Subsequently, the imaging was received and it was
reviewed by Dr. ___ in Radiology.  Other diagnostic 
mammogram
in ___ of the small coarse heterogeneous calcifications in
the lower outer subareolar right breast were noted, which were
not significantly changed in comparison to prior studies.  There
was, however, new spiculated mass in the upper inner left breast
at middle depth for which further imaging was recommended. 
Ultrasound was reviewed at the region of the 11 to 12 o'clock
position, 5 cm from the nipple, there was a 1.1 x 1.0 x 0.7 cm
hypoechoic mass with indistinct margins corresponding to the
mammographic mass.  This was subsequently biopsied and clip was
placed within the mass.  A single image of the left axilla was
reviewed that did not show any abnormal-appearing lymph nodes. 
An MRI was recommended to further assess the bilateral breasts
due to the aforementioned findings.

She did have an MRI on ___.  A round mass with
irregular margins and heterogeneous enhancement was noted in the
upper inner quadrant of the left breast measuring 1.3 x 1.2 x 
1.1
cm in size corresponding to the biopsy-proven carcinoma.  No
adenopathy was noted.  No other abnormalities were identified. 
No MRI evidence of malignancy within the right breast.

Her pathology as well was not available at the time of our
initial consultation in clinic.  More recently, this has become
available and the biopsy on ___, was reviewed by Dr.
___ in our ___ Department.  The left breast lesion at
the 11 to 12 o'clock position, 5 cm from the nipple, there is an
invasive carcinoma with predominant lobular features noted, 
grade
2 with ER positive, PR positive and HER-2/neu negative per
report.

Ms. ___ did meet with Dr. ___ in Plastic ___ to discuss
reconstructive options on ___, as we discussed
mastectomy, the standard of care in this clinical situation. 
However, she has decided not to proceed with reconstruction at
this time.

We did discuss her case at the tumor board conference on ___.  The multidisciplinary group recommendations were to omit 
a
sentinel lymph node biopsy given that an axillary lymph node
dissection previously done on ___, revealing 17 lymph
nodes and also thereafter, she had received radiation therapy. 
Given her age and the previous axillary lymph node dissection 
and
radiation treatment to the axilla, it was thought that sentinel
lymph node biopsy would not be necessary for the adjuvant 
therapy
decision making.

I am in favor of omitting the sentinel lymph node biopsy as 
well.

We did discuss her upcoming surgical plan with Dr. ___ vascular surgeon who is following her for chronic SMA
dissection.  Dr. ___ her with an annual
ultrasound.  He reports there are no concerns or issues from his
standpoint for us to proceed with a planned mastectomy for the
recurrent left breast cancer.  He does recommend control of her
blood pressure and that will be achieved by anesthesia
colleagues.

Ms. ___ unfortunately does report she had a recent accident
in swimming pool.  She was trying to get out of the pool and the
water was not available and as she was being lifted up she
unfortunately hit her chest and abdomen against the side of the
pool.  She reports that she had significant chest discomfort and
was evaluated at ___.  Per her report, there
were no acute issues from the injury; however, she started to
have soreness over the chest wall particularly on the right 
side.
 Though the issue of concern is that her GJ tube appears not to
be quite top against her skin as it was before and there was 
some
discomfort at the site.  She is going to be seeing her physician
in ___ later today to ask if she would need
any further evaluation of the GJ tube.

in dry 4x4, tegaderm- c/d/I. JP drain in place, serosanguinous

 CV: RRR, No M/G/R

 ABD: Soft, nondistended, nontender, no rebound or guarding,

 Ext: No ___ edema, ___ warm and well perfused

Brief Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the breast surgery service for 
overnight observation after undergoing a total left mastectomy 
for recurrent left breast cancer (grade 2 invasive lobular 
carcinoma, ER/PR+) previously treated with lumpectomy and 
radiation therapy. The procedure was uncomplicated (see 
Operative Report for further details) and a single drain was 
left in place in the left chest to bulb suction. The patient did 
well post-operatively in the PACU and was transferred to the 
floor in stable condition. She voided appropriately, tolerated 
first clears then a regular diet, and had her pain well 
controlled on oral agents. Use of narcotic analgesia was 
minimized in order to prevent exacerbation of her severe 
gastroperesis. Instead, she received Tylenol and tramadol, as 
needed, with good relief. She ambulated, wore SCDs, and used the 
incentive spirometer effectively. She was afebrile and 
hemodynamically stable throughout her hospital course. She was 
discharged home on POD1 in good condition with visiting nurse 
services set up for drain care. She will be seen for follow up 
in breast surgery clinic in one week.

5.  Citalopram 40 mg PO DAILY

8.  LORazepam 1 mg PO QHS  
9.  Omeprazole 20 mg PO DAILY  

 
Discharge Disposition:
Home With Service

Discharge Diagnosis:
left breast cancer

 
Discharge Condition:
Mental Status: Clear and coherent.
Level of Consciousness: Alert and interactive.
Activity Status: Ambulatory - Independent.

 
Discharge Instructions:
You were admitted to the breast surgery service after undergoing 
a left total mastectomy (removal of all your left breast 
tissue). Your procedure went well and you did well 
post-operatively. You are being discharged home in stable 
condition with visiting nursing services for your drain. 

Please follow the directions below;

Personal Care: 
1. You may remove your surgical dressing after 48 hours and 
leave your incision open to air.
2. Clean around the drain site(s), where the tubing exits the 
skin, with soap and water. 
3. Strip drain tubing, empty bulb(s), and record output(s) ___ 
times per day. 
4. A written record of the daily output from your drain should 
be brought to every follow-up appointment. Your drain will be 
removed as soon as possible when the daily output tapers off to 
an acceptable amount. 
5. You may shower daily. No baths until instructed to do so by 
Dr. ___.
6. You may wear a soft, non-restrictive camisole but no tight or 
underwire bras. 

Activity: 
1. You may resume your regular diet. 
2. DO NOT lift anything heavier than 5 pounds or engage in 
strenuous activity for two weeks. 

Medications: 
1. Resume your regular medications unless instructed otherwise 
and take any new meds as ordered. 
2. You may take your prescribed pain medication for moderate to 
severe pain. You may switch to Tylenol or Extra Strength Tylenol 
for mild pain as directed on the packaging. Please note that 
Percocet and Vicodin have Tylenol as an active ingredient so do 
not take these meds with additional Tylenol. 
3. Take prescription pain medications (tramadol) for pain not 
relieved by tylenol.
4.Take Colace, 100 mg by mouth 2 times per day, while taking the 
prescription pain medication. You may use a different 
over-the-counter stool softener if you wish. 
5. Do not drive or operate heavy machinery while taking any 
narcotic pain medication. You may have constipation when taking 
narcotic pain medications (tramadol, oxycodone, percocet, 
vicodin, hydrocodone, dilaudid, etc.); you should continue 
drinking fluids, you may take stool softeners, and should eat 
foods that are high in fiber. 

Call the office IMMEDIATELY if you have any of the following: 
1. Signs of infection: fever with chills, increased redness, 
swelling, warmth or tenderness at the surgical site, or unusual 
drainage from the incision(s). 
2. A large amount of bleeding from the incision(s) or drain(s). 
3. Fever greater than 101.5 oF 
4. Severe pain NOT relieved by your medication. 

Return to the ER if: 
* If you are vomiting and cannot keep in fluids or your 
medications. 
* If you have shaking chills, fever greater than 101.5 (F) 
degrees or 38 (C) degrees, increased redness, swelling or 
discharge from incision, chest pain, shortness of breath, or 
anything else that is troubling you. 
* Any serious change in your symptoms, or any new symptoms that 
concern you. 

DRAIN DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS 
You are being discharged with drains in place. Drain care is a 
clean procedure. Wash your hands thoroughly with soap and warm 
water before performing drain care. Perform drainage care twice 
a day. Try to empty the drain at the same time each day. Pull 
the stopper out of the drainage bottle and empty the drainage 
fluid into the measuring cup. Record the amount of drainage 
fluid on the record sheet. Reestablish drain suction.
Thank you for allowing us to participate in your care.
 
Followup Instructions:
___

conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Ms. ___. I’m Dr. ___, part of the breast surgery team. You’re here today for your scheduled left total mastectomy due to recurrent breast cancer. How are you feeling this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m a little nervous, but I’m ready to get this done. I’ve been through this before, so I know what to expect, more or less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. You’ve had a lumpectomy and radiation before, correct? And no signs of recurrence until now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. It was over ten years ago. I’ve been followed closely, and then this new mass showed up on my mammogram.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the imaging showed a new spiculated mass in the upper inner quadrant. The biopsy confirmed invasive lobular carcinoma, grade 2. The good news is it’s ER and PR positive, which gives us good treatment options later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And HER2 negative, right? That’s what my oncologist said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. HER2 negative. That means we won’t use drugs like Herceptin, but hormone therapy will likely be part of your plan after surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve been on tamoxifen before. Will I go back on something like that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Your medical oncologist will decide that after reviewing the final pathology. For now, we’re proceeding with the mastectomy. We discussed skipping the sentinel lymph node biopsy—does that still sound okay to you?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Since I already had the full node dissection and radiation, it seems unnecessary to do it again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The tumor board agreed. It wouldn’t change treatment decisions, and it adds risk without benefit in your case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I also wanted to mention—I had a little accident last week in the pool.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I saw that in your history. You hit your chest and abdomen getting out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. No broken bones, but my GJ tube site has been a bit sore. It doesn’t sit as flush as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep an eye on that. The surgical site is on the left, and your GJ tube is on the abdomen, so they’re separate. But we’ll make sure your gastroparesis is managed carefully—no heavy narcotics that could slow things further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m used to that. I take Reglan and Zofran at home. Will I be able to restart those soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll start clear liquids once you’re awake and then advance as tolerated. We’ll restart your meds as soon as you can take them by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my thyroid and anxiety meds too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. All your regular medications will be resumed unless there’s a specific reason not to. We’ve got your list: Celexa, Synthroid, lorazepam, gabapentin, omeprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I get anxious if I miss my lorazepam at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you get it. Now, the surgery should take about two hours. You’ll wake up in the PACU with a drain in place to collect fluid from the surgical site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One drain? Last time I had two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This time, one should be enough. We’ll monitor the output. Once it drops below 30 cc per day for two days, we can remove it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I’ll have help with it at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, visiting nurse services will come to assist with drain care and check your incision. You’ll also have a follow-up appointment in one week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I live alone, so that helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you’re not alone in this. Any other questions before we head to the OR?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m ready. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Ms. ___, welcome back. The surgery went very well. You’ve had a left total mastectomy, and the incision looks clean. You have one JP drain in place, and your vitals are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How do I feel? Sore, but okay. Is the drain hurting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might feel a little tugging, but we’ve given you acetaminophen and tramadol for pain. We’re avoiding strong narcotics because of your gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Smart. Morphine really slows me down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We want you up and moving to prevent complications. You’ll wear compression sleeves and use the incentive spirometer every hour while awake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. Deep breaths to keep my lungs clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And we’ll start you on clear liquids soon—water, broth. If you tolerate that, we’ll move to a regular diet tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have my Reglan and Zofran tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Once you’re tolerating liquids, yes. We’ll start them this evening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You did great overnight. You’re afebrile, pain is controlled, and you’ve been eating a regular diet. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll remove the dressing in 48 hours and keep the incision open to air. Clean around the drain site with soap and water, empty the bulb twice daily, and record the output.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no lifting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nothing heavier than five pounds for two weeks. No driving while on tramadol. And call us if you have fever, increased redness, or severe pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my GJ tube? Should I be worried about the discomfort?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely just bruising from the fall. Keep the site clean. If it becomes red, swollen, or starts draining, call your GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my follow-up is in one week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and the visiting nurse will help until then. You’re doing really well, Ms. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel lucky to have such a good team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad to take care of you. Let’s get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—will I need chemotherapy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That decision will be made by your oncologist based on the final pathology. Since it’s ER/PR positive and HER2 negative, hormone therapy is likely, but chemo may not be needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope not. I really didn’t tolerate it well last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discuss all options at your follow-up. For now, focus on healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember—rest, follow the instructions, and we’ll see you next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. Have a safe trip home.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of breast cancer, gastroparesis, and a GJ tube presented for a left total mastectomy due to recurrent invasive lobular carcinoma in the upper-inner quadrant, ER/PR positive and HER2 negative. The surgery was uncomplicated, and she was admitted for overnight observation. Pain was managed with acetaminophen and tramadol to avoid exacerbating gastroparesis. She tolerated a clear diet postoperatively and advanced to a regular diet, remained afebrile, and was ambulating well. A single JP drain was placed, and visiting nurse services were arranged for home care. She was discharged on postoperative day one with instructions for wound and drain care, activity restrictions, and a follow-up appointment in one week. Final pathology is pending, and further oncologic treatment will be determined in consultation with medical oncology.
